findings.title: Pin and verify the installer before execution
findings.whyItBreaks: Every image build downloads mutable content and immediately executes it as root. A compromised server, DNS/TLS endpoint, or changed response can inject arbitrary code into the produced image, while identical source revisions may produce different artifacts.

findings.title: Make installer download failures abort the build
findings.whyItBreaks: Docker runs this pipeline through /bin/sh, whose pipeline status is the status of the final `sh` process. If curl fails before producing input, `sh` can exit successfully on empty input, so the image build succeeds without installing the required component. HTTP failures are also not rejected because curl lacks `--fail`.

findings.title: Pin and verify the remotely executed installer
findings.whyItBreaks: Every image build downloads and executes whatever https://example.com/install.sh serves at that moment. The URL has no immutable version, digest, or signature verification, so compromise or replacement of the remote content gives the publisher arbitrary code execution in the build environment and produces non-reproducible images.

findings.title: Propagate installer download failures
findings.whyItBreaks: Docker runs this pipeline through /bin/sh without pipefail, so its status is the status of `sh`, not `curl`. If curl fails before producing input, `sh` can exit successfully on an empty script and the image build continues without the required installation.

findings.title: Preserve curl failures instead of masking them in the pipeline
findings.whyItBreaks: Docker's shell-form RUN observes the status of the final `sh` process. If curl fails before producing input, `sh` can exit successfully after reading an empty stream, so the image build continues without the intended installation.

findings.title: Preserve the missing-key failure signal
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing when the key is absent, but LoadOrDefault discards that error and returns "". Its public contract therefore forces callers to treat a missing key exactly like a present key whose legitimate value is empty; no caller can recover the lost distinction.

findings.title: Preserve load failures in the exported wrapper
findings.whyItBreaks: Discarding Load's error makes a missing or failed lookup indistinguishable from a successfully stored empty string. Because LoadOrDefault is exported and returns no error or presence indicator, every caller is forced to treat failure as valid data.

findings.title: Preserve the missing-key error
findings.whyItBreaks: Ignoring Load's error makes a missing key indistinguishable from a present key whose value is an empty string. Because LoadOrDefault is exported and returns no status, every caller is forced to treat lookup failure as successful empty data.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Each send now runs in a detached goroutine, so Run can return while results are still pending. A caller that closes the results channel after Run returns can trigger a send-on-closed-channel panic; a caller that treats return as completion can also observe missing results. The previous implementation returned only after every send completed.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Each send now runs in an untracked goroutine, so Run returns as soon as the goroutines are launched. A caller that closes or stops consuming results after Run returns can cause send-on-closed-channel panics or permanently blocked goroutines. Previously, returning guaranteed that every result had been sent.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Each send now runs in an untracked goroutine, so Run can return while sends remain pending. A caller that closes results after Run returns—previously safe because all sends had completed—can cause those goroutines to panic with "send on closed channel". The change also removes the prior completion guarantee.

findings.title: Preserve the exported Log function type
findings.whyItBreaks: Although ordinary Log("message") calls remain valid, Go function types require exact signatures. Existing consumers such as `var log func(string) = logger.Log` compile against the base version but fail after Log becomes `func(string, ...string)`.

findings.title: Preserve Log's existing function type
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing Log from func(string) to func(string, ...string) remains compatible with direct one-argument calls, but breaks consumers that assign or pass logger.Log where func(string) is required. The new tag parameter is unused, so the compatibility break adds no observable functionality.

findings.title: Preserve compatibility with the original Log function type
findings.whyItBreaks: Although existing direct calls such as Log("message") still compile, the exported function no longer has type func(string). Existing consumers that assign logger.Log to a func(string) variable, callback, or interface field will fail to compile after upgrading.

findings.title: Restore tenant-scoped admin checks before deleting records
findings.whyItBreaks: Replacing AND with OR authorizes two previously forbidden destructive paths: any non-admin may delete records in their tenant, and any admin may delete records belonging to another tenant. Either path bypasses an independent authorization boundary and can cause unauthorized data loss.

findings.title: Restore both deletion authorization requirements
findings.whyItBreaks: The predicate now returns true for a non-admin in the record's tenant and for an admin from a different tenant. Either case bypasses one of the two previously mandatory authorization checks and can permit unauthorized record deletion.

findings.title: Restore conjunctive tenant-admin authorization
findings.whyItBreaks: Using OR grants deletion when either condition holds: a non-admin in the record's tenant now passes, and an admin from another tenant also passes. Both cases were rejected previously, creating direct authorization bypass and data-loss paths.

findings.title: Preserve parse failures instead of overwriting settings
findings.whyItBreaks: Malformed JSON and invalid fields previously propagated an error. They now return DEFAULTS, so updateFontSize cannot distinguish failure from valid default-valued settings and saves a replacement object, silently resetting the user's theme while changing the font size. The exported parseSettings API also forces every caller to conflate invalid input with legitimate defaults.

findings.title: Preserve parse failures instead of overwriting settings
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch converts every JSON or validation failure into DEFAULTS. updateFontSize then treats those defaults as successfully parsed data and saves them. For example, {"theme":"dark","fontSize":"large"} now becomes {"theme":"light","fontSize":16}, silently losing the valid theme; previously the error reached updateFontSize and save was not called. The exported parseSettings API also no longer lets callers distinguish invalid input from genuine default-valued settings.

findings.title: Preserve parse failures instead of returning defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Malformed JSON or an invalid field previously propagated an exception and prevented saving. It now produces a valid-looking default Settings object, so updateFontSize continues and saves the requested size with theme reset to "light". Callers of the exported parser also cannot distinguish corrupted input from genuine default settings.

findings.title: Fetch artifacts from the reported branch commit
findings.whyItBreaks: When the requested branch and "verified" resolve to different commits, builtFrom identifies the branch commit while artifacts are fetched from the verified commit. Consumers therefore receive a self-inconsistent report and may publish or attribute the wrong artifacts.

findings.title: Look up artifacts at the reported commit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any branch whose commit differs from the "verified" ref, builtFrom identifies the requested branch commit while artifacts contains files from another commit. The extra ref lookup can also break reports when that ref does not exist.

findings.title: Fetch artifacts from the requested branch commit
findings.whyItBreaks: When the requested branch and "verified" resolve to different commits, builtFrom identifies the branch commit while artifacts contains files from the verified commit. The resulting report is internally inconsistent and can attribute the wrong artifacts to a build.

findings.title: Restore the positive-limit slice
findings.whyItBreaks: For every positive limit, the function now returns the entire reversed input. For example, recentEntries(["old", "mid", "new"], 2) returns three entries rather than two. renderFeed passes 20, so inputs longer than 20 also expand its output beyond 20 elements.

findings.title: Restore the positive-limit slice
findings.whyItBreaks: For every positive limit, recentEntries now returns the entire reversed input. renderFeed passes 20, so an input with more than 20 entries makes the assignment loop extend `out` beyond its initial length and returns an oversized feed, violating both the helper contract and renderFeed's page size.

findings.title: Restore the positive-limit slice
findings.whyItBreaks: For every positive limit, the function now returns the entire reversed input. For example, renderFeed passes 20, but an input with 21 entries produces a 21-element result because assignments beyond the initially allocated array extend it. This violates the exported function's at-most-limit contract.

findings.title: Count only entries emitted into the manifest
findings.whyItBreaks: Stale entries are removed from the rows, but headerLines still receives entries.length. For one live and one stale entry, the manifest declares '# entry-count: 2' while containing only one entry row, so consumers validating or preallocating from the count receive contradictory data.

findings.title: Count only the entries written to the manifest
findings.whyItBreaks: When any entry is stale, the data rows contain only live entries while `# entry-count` still uses `entries.length`. The public manifest therefore declares more entries than it contains, breaking consumers that validate or use the count.

findings.title: Count only the live manifest entries
findings.whyItBreaks: When any entry is stale, rows are generated from the filtered `live` array while `# entry-count` still uses `entries.length`. For example, one live and one stale entry produces one row but declares two, violating the manifest's count contract.

findings.title: Restore the exported legacy formatter
findings.whyItBreaks: FormatLegacyID is an exported package API. Its removal makes any downstream package still calling ids.FormatLegacyID fail to compile on upgrade, with no compatibility shim or replacement provided.

findings.title: Preserve the exported legacy formatter
findings.whyItBreaks: FormatLegacyID is an exported package API. Deleting it makes every existing external caller fail to compile with undefined: ids.FormatLegacyID, even though the legacy formatting behavior was previously supported and tested.

findings.title: Restore the shippingQuote export
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, src/orders.ts publicly exported shippingQuote. It now only imports quoteShipping privately, so existing consumers importing shippingQuote from this module fail to compile or load after upgrading.

findings.title: Preserve the shippingQuote export from orders
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, consumers could import shippingQuote from src/orders.ts. The replacement imports quoteShipping privately and does not re-export either name, so every existing consumer of shippingQuote fails to compile or load after upgrading even though equivalent functionality still exists in another module.

findings.title: Preserve the shippingQuote export
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing consumers importing shippingQuote from src/orders now fail because that exported function was removed. The equivalent implementation is only available under the new quoteShipping name in a different module, so this refactor introduces a source-level upgrade break.

findings.title: Reject invalid stored hashes without raising
findings.whyItBreaks: hmac.compare_digest requires compatible types and ASCII-only strings. Values such as None, bytes, or non-ASCII text previously compared unequal and caused guard() to return 401, but now raise TypeError and turn authentication failure into an unhandled server error.

findings.title: Reject malformed stored hashes before compare_digest
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous string equality returned false for a non-string or non-ASCII stored_hash, so guard returned 401. hmac.compare_digest raises TypeError for mixed types and non-ASCII strings, causing the authentication guard to fail with an exception instead of denying access.

findings.title: Restore execute's string result
findings.whyItBreaks: Every invocation of the public execute function now throws "always fails". The base implementation returned the uppercased input, and the unchanged public signature still promises a string result, so this is an unconditional behavioral and contract regression.

findings.title: Restore execute's string transformation
findings.whyItBreaks: execute previously returned input.toUpperCase() for every string, but the changed implementation unconditionally throws. Every consumer of this exported API therefore loses its result and encounters an exception instead.

findings.title: Restore the exported operation's result
findings.whyItBreaks: Every call to the public execute function now throws "always fails" for every valid string, replacing the previous uppercase result and making the exported API unusable.

findings.title: Allow active viewers to reach the read-only path
findings.whyItBreaks: For an active viewer below the attempt limit, isEligible now returns false, so handle returns "rejected" at line 24. The viewer-specific "read-only" result at line 25 can no longer be reached, regressing a legitimately supported action.

findings.title: Preserve the read-only viewer path
findings.whyItBreaks: For an active viewer with fewer than five attempts, isEligible now returns false, so handle returns "rejected" at line 24. The intended "read-only" result at line 25 is therefore unreachable.

findings.title: Keep viewers eligible for read-only handling
findings.whyItBreaks: For an active viewer below the attempt limit, this new guard returns false. handle() consequently returns "rejected" at line 24, making its intended "read-only" viewer result at line 25 unreachable.

findings.title: Allow unpaid drafts to be saved
findings.whyItBreaks: For {state: "draft", payment: "missing"}, canProceed changed from true to false. saveDraft therefore returns "blocked" instead of "saved", although saving a draft is independent of payment completion.

With order={state:"draft", payment:"missing"}, the new payment condition returns false, so saveDraft returns "blocked" instead of "saved". Payment can legitimately govern submission, but it must not prevent preserving an unpaid draft.

findings.title: Load snapshot files from the selected channel head
findings.whyItBreaks: When the requested channel and stable point to different commits, the returned Snapshot reports the requested channel's commit but contains files from stable. Consumers therefore publish or display an internally inconsistent snapshot.

findings.title: Read files from the requested channel's commit
findings.whyItBreaks: For every non-stable channel, the returned Snapshot identifies `head` as its commit but contains files loaded from the stable commit. Consumers therefore receive internally inconsistent snapshot data, and publishing also fails unnecessarily when the stable ref is absent.

findings.title: Load files from the requested channel's commit
findings.whyItBreaks: When the requested channel differs from stable, the returned snapshot identifies the requested channel's head commit but contains files from stable. Consumers therefore receive an internally inconsistent snapshot and may publish the wrong contents.

findings.title: Honor the requested build limit
findings.whyItBreaks: The public function now accepts a limit argument, but its body still iterates over the hard-coded max_count of 10. For example, build("x", limit=2) returns 10 items instead of 2.

findings.title: Honor the new limit argument
findings.whyItBreaks: The public signature now promises a configurable limit, but the body still iterates over the hard-coded max_count of 10. Calls such as build("x", limit=3) therefore return 10 items instead of 3.

findings.title: Honor the new limit parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: The signature promises callers can control the output limit, but the body still assigns max_count = 10 and iterates range(max_count). For example, build("x", limit=2) returns 10 elements instead of 2.

findings.title: Reject non-positive values in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: The new public name promises a positive integer, but int(value) accepts 0 and negative values. Consequently, charge("-1") returns -100 and charge("0") returns 0 instead of rejecting invalid charge amounts.

findings.title: Reject non-positive values in parse_positive_int

findings.title: Reject non-positive values in parse_positive_int

findings.title: Preserve the input DataFrame instead of mutating it
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation updated a defensive copy, so callers could retain and reuse the original DataFrame unchanged. Assigning through df.loc now modifies that caller-owned object in place; both the input and returned object contain the updates, which is a behavioral regression for callers relying on the established non-mutating contract.

findings.title: Borrow items in the debug statement

findings.whyItBreaks: The deferred Close return value is discarded. When WriteString and Flush succeed but Close reports a delayed filesystem or I/O failure, this exported function now returns nil. Callers are therefore forced to treat an incompletely persisted file as successfully saved; before this change, the error reached the caller through `return f.Close()`.

findings.title: Iterate through the full half-open page window
findings.whyItBreaks: The computed end is already exclusive, but subtracting one from it makes range() omit the page's final row. A full two-row page returns only its first row, and every page of size 1 is empty. render_page and summarize inherit the data loss.

findings.title: Preserve the existing public keyword parameter names
findings.whyItBreaks: All five public functions rename parameters without a compatibility layer. Existing valid calls such as clamp(n=1, lo=0, hi=2), page_count(total=10, size=5), or summarize(rows=[], size=5) now raise TypeError even though their positional behavior is intended to remain equivalent.

findings.title: Include the final row in each page window
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns a half-open [start, end) interval, but range(start, end - 1) excludes both end and end - 1. Every non-empty page loses its final row; pages of size 1 become empty. render_page and summarize propagate the truncated output.

findings.title: Preserve the existing public keyword parameter names
findings.whyItBreaks: The public signatures rename n/lo/hi, total/size, and page/size. Existing callers using keywords such as clamp(n=..., lo=..., hi=...), page_count(total=..., size=...), or summarize(size=...) now raise TypeError instead of producing a result. No compatibility shim or migration path is present.

findings.title: Iterate through the half-open end bound
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns an exclusive end, but subtracting one before range excludes the final row of every page. For rows=[a,b,c] and page_size=2, page 0 returns only a and page 1 returns nothing; page_size=1 makes every page empty. render_page and summarize therefore silently omit data.

findings.title: Preserve the existing public keyword names
findings.whyItBreaks: All public function parameters were renamed. Existing Python callers using supported keyword syntax such as clamp(n=1, lo=0, hi=2), page_count(total=10, size=5), or summarize(rows, size=5) now raise TypeError instead of returning a result.

findings.title: Restore the TTL comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: A newly stored entry has age <= ttlMs, so get() deletes it and returns null. Once its age exceeds ttlMs, the same condition returns the expired value. This reverses the cache's intended behavior.

findings.title: Remove completed jobs without splicing during iteration
findings.whyItBreaks: Splicing shifts the next element into the current index, but forEach advances to the following index. For two adjacent completed jobs, the second is skipped and remains in the returned array; the function also newly mutates its caller's array.

findings.title: Restore the TTL validity comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: A freshly stored entry has age 0, so the new `>` comparison rejects and deletes it. Conversely, an expired entry satisfies the comparison and is returned indefinitely. This makes the cache unusable for normal positive TTL values.

findings.title: Avoid splicing the array while iterating forward
findings.whyItBreaks: After `splice` removes a completed job, the next element shifts into the current index, but `forEach` advances past it. For `[done, done]`, the second completed job remains in the returned queue.

findings.title: Restore the TTL comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Fresh entries now fail the condition, are deleted, and return null, while entries older than ttlMs are returned indefinitely. This reverses the cache's expiration behavior.

findings.title: Avoid splicing while iterating completed jobs
findings.whyItBreaks: Splicing shifts the next element left while forEach advances its index, so consecutive completed jobs are skipped. For `[done, done]`, the function leaves one completed job in the result. It also regresses the previous non-mutating behavior.

findings.title: Preserve the empty-input result
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the empty-array guard changes averageAmount([]) from 0 to NaN because it computes 0 / 0. This is an observable regression in an exported function and can contaminate downstream arithmetic or serialization.

findings.title: Sort a copy instead of mutating the input
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() operates in place, so merely asking for the busiest row now reorders the caller's rows array. Callers retaining input order will observe silently corrupted state; the previous implementation deliberately sorted a copy.

findings.title: Preserve the zero result for empty input
findings.whyItBreaks: For an empty array, total is 0 and rows.length is 0, so this now returns NaN instead of the previous public result of 0. Callers performing arithmetic or serialization receive an invalid value.

findings.title: Avoid mutating the caller's row order
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort operates in place. Unlike the previous defensive-copy implementation, calling busiest now permanently reorders the caller's array, so subsequent code observes rows in descending amount order.

findings.title: Restore the empty-input result
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the empty-array guard makes averageAmount([]) evaluate 0 / 0 and return NaN instead of the previous documented-by-behavior result of 0. NaN can then contaminate arithmetic or serialized output.

findings.title: Do not reorder the caller's rows
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort mutates rows in place. The previous defensive copy preserved caller order, so callers that reuse the array now observe an unexpected descending reorder after merely requesting the busiest row.

findings.title: Restore numeric score ordering
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() without a comparator converts scores to strings. For players ordered with scores [2, 10] and n=1, rankScores returns [2, 10], making the cutoff 2; filtering and slicing then returns the score-2 player instead of the score-10 player.

findings.title: Restore numeric descending score sorting
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() compares scores as strings. For scores [9, 80, 100], reversing the default ordering produces [9, 80, 100], so topPlayers(..., 1) uses 9 as the cutoff and can return the first low-scoring player instead of the player scoring 100.

findings.title: Restore numeric score sorting
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() compares values as strings without a comparator. Scores [2, 10, 9] become [9, 2, 10] after sort and reverse, producing cutoff 2 for n=2; topPlayers then returns scores [2, 10] and omits the actual second-place score 9.

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Replacing hmac.compare_digest with == makes comparison timing depend on where the supplied signature differs. A remote attacker able to collect enough webhook response timings can use this side channel to infer a valid HMAC and reach the authenticated processor path.

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Python string equality may return after the first mismatching character, making response timing correlate with the matching signature prefix. An attacker able to collect repeated webhook timings can use that signal to progressively forge a valid signature and reach the processor.

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Ordinary string equality can return sooner based on the first mismatching character. A remote attacker able to collect enough webhook response timings can use that signal to infer a valid HMAC incrementally and reach the authenticated processor path.

findings.title: Keep balance updates inside the transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The transaction now commits immediately after the ledger insert. If either subsequent account update fails, the ledger entry remains committed; if the credit update fails after the debit succeeds, the transfer also leaves balances partially updated. Previously all three writes rolled back together.

findings.title: Keep ledger and balance writes in one transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The transaction commits immediately after the ledger insert. If either subsequent balance update fails, the ledger entry remains committed while balances are unchanged or partially updated, leaving financial state inconsistent. Previously all three writes rolled back together.

findings.title: Keep balance updates inside the transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The transaction commits immediately after the ledger insert. If either subsequent balance update raises or the process stops, the ledger entry remains committed while one or both account balances remain unchanged, leaving financial state inconsistent. Previously all three writes rolled back together.

findings.title: Keep billing dates in UTC
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation consistently derived the billing date in UTC. The new local-time getters change results according to the server timezone: for example, 2026-09-06T16:30:00Z produces 2026-09-07 under Asia/Taipei instead of 2026-09-06. This also makes sameBillingDay misclassify timestamps around local midnight and causes deployments in different timezones to disagree.

findings.title: Preserve UTC when deriving the billing day
findings.whyItBreaks: Replacing the UTC getters with local-time getters makes the exported result depend on the process timezone. For example, 2024-01-01T16:00:00Z produces 2024-01-01 under the previous implementation but 2024-01-02 under TZ=Asia/Taipei. This also makes sameBillingDay return false for UTC-same-day instants that straddle local midnight.

findings.title: Restore UTC calendar fields for billing days
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation deliberately used UTC getters. With TZ=America/Los_Angeles, 2026-01-01T00:30:00Z now produces 2025-12-31 rather than 2026-01-01. Identical instants therefore receive different billing keys on hosts with different timezones, and sameBillingDay can misclassify dates around midnight.

findings.title: Keep the tenant in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: After readProfile("tenant-a", "user", ...) caches a profile, readProfile("tenant-b", "user", ...) uses the same key and returns tenant A's profile at line 16 without invoking the tenant-B fetch. This exposes incorrect and potentially tenant-confidential profile data.

findings.title: Restore the tenant component of the cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: Two tenants using the same account identifier now share one cache entry. After readProfile("tenant-a", "alice", fetchProfile) caches tenant A's profile, the same call for tenant B returns that cached Profile without invoking fetchProfile, exposing tenant A's data and reporting the wrong tenant.

findings.title: Restore tenant isolation in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: After tenant A caches account X, readProfile for tenant B and account X hits the same key and returns tenant A's Profile without invoking fetchProfile. This exposes incorrect, potentially tenant-private profile data across tenants.

findings.title: Preserve the load failure signal
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported load API previously threw when the key was missing and propagated errors from store.get. It now returns "" for both failures, which is indistinguishable from a successfully stored empty string, forcing every caller to treat failures as valid data.

findings.title: Preserve load failures instead of returning an empty value
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch converts both the explicit missing-key error and any exception thrown by store.get into "". Because an empty string is also a valid stored value, callers cannot distinguish failure from successful retrieval. loadAll likewise returns an apparently successful array containing "" where it previously propagated the error.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key failures instead of returning an empty value
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported load API previously threw when a key was absent, but now returns "". Because "" is also a valid Map<string, string> value, callers cannot distinguish failure from stored data. loadAll consequently turns a missing key into an apparently successful array element instead of propagating the error. The catch also suppresses any exception thrown by store.get.

findings.title: Preserve the timeoutMs configuration contract
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing TypeScript consumers using the exported Config shape no longer compile because timeoutMs was removed and retries became mandatory. Existing untyped JavaScript callers pass no timeout property, so line 8 calculates NaN and the deadline predicate never stops retries.

findings.title: Perform the initial attempt before counting retries
findings.whyItBreaks: The public retries field denotes retries after an initial attempt, but it is used as the total-attempt loop bound. retries=0 never calls fn, and retries=1 permits only the initial call rather than one retry.

findings.title: Propagate failure after background retries are exhausted
findings.whyItBreaks: Every exception from fn is discarded and retryBackground returns void both on success and after exhaustion. Because this is an exported API, callers are forced to treat a failed operation as successful and cannot safely report, persist, or retry the failure.

findings.title: Preserve the existing Config contract
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing TypeScript consumers using { maxAttempts, timeoutMs } no longer compile because timeoutMs was removed and retries became required. Existing untyped JavaScript consumers pass undefined as config.timeout, producing a NaN deadline; the deadline guard is then always false and silently stops enforcing the configured timeout.

findings.title: Count retries after the initial attempt
findings.whyItBreaks: The public field is named retries, but the loop treats it as total attempts. retries=0 never invokes fn, while retries=2 permits only two total attempts instead of one initial attempt plus two retries.

findings.title: Propagate retryBackground exhaustion failures
findings.whyItBreaks: Every callback exception is caught, and after the final failed attempt the exported function returns normally. Callers are forced to treat exhausted failure as successful void completion and cannot report, retry, or compensate for the failed operation.

findings.title: Preserve the existing Config fields
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing TypeScript callers using { maxAttempts, timeoutMs } no longer compile because timeoutMs was removed and retries became required. Uncompiled JavaScript callers are worse: config.timeout is undefined, producing a NaN deadline, so the timeout guard never stops retries.

findings.title: Propagate the final background retry failure
findings.whyItBreaks: After the last callback failure, the exported function returns normally with undefined. Callers cannot distinguish exhausted retries from a successful void callback and can report or persist failed work as successful.

findings.title: Convert numeric values before reading their length
findings.whyItBreaks: `FieldProps.value` now permits numbers, but numbers have no `length` property. TypeScript rejects the component, and transpile-only execution renders `len=undefined` for a valid numeric prop.

findings.title: Handle numeric values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: `FieldProps.value` now permits `number`, but numbers have no `length` property. TypeScript rejects the component, and emitted JavaScript would render `len=undefined` for a valid numeric prop.

findings.title: Handle numeric values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: FieldProps now publicly permits numbers, but numbers have no length property. TypeScript rejects this expression; if emitted anyway, rendering value={42} produces "len=undefined" instead of a meaningful label.

findings.title: Remove the deployment token from workflow output
findings.whyItBreaks: Shell expansion sends the raw TOKEN value to stdout and therefore into the Actions logging pipeline. GitHub's secret masking is defense-in-depth, not authorization to emit credentials; masking limitations or downstream log handling can disclose the deployment token.

findings.title: Restore the enlarged git output buffer
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer restores spawnSync's 1 MiB default. The git helper captures the complete PR patch at line 140, so any diff exceeding that limit terminates with ENOBUFS and the entire review fails instead of producing a verdict. The previous 64 MiB limit explicitly supported these inputs.

findings.title: Keep baseSha aligned with the generated patch
findings.whyItBreaks: The patch and changed-file set are computed from mergeBase, but the bundle now labels the target branch tip as baseSha. When the target branch advanced after the PR diverged, baseSha and mergeBase differ; consumers receive metadata claiming a B..H comparison while the supplied patch is M..H. Reconstructing or inspecting the comparison from the advertised SHAs then includes base-only changes as apparent PR reversions.

findings.title: Restore the larger buffer for Git output
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync now uses Node's default 1 MiB maxBuffer. runGithub captures the complete `git diff` through this helper at line 140, so a valid PR whose patch exceeds 1 MiB terminates the subprocess and causes the review to enter the failure path instead of producing a result. The adjacent GitHub helpers retain a 64 MiB limit, making this a direct regression in large-PR support.

findings.title: Restore the Git output buffer limit
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer restores spawnSync's 1 MiB default. The git diff at line 140 can legitimately exceed that size; spawnSync then fails with ENOBUFS, status is nonzero/null, and runGithub records a failed check instead of reviewing the PR.

findings.title: Keep Codex executions in the read-only sandbox
findings.whyItBreaks: Without `-s read-only`, Codex resolves its sandbox from ambient defaults or user configuration. A workspace-write or danger-full-access configuration therefore lets an untrusted repository influence the reviewer into modifying files or executing write-capable commands inside `opts.repoPath`, breaking the reviewer's read-only security boundary.

findings.title: Restore the explicit read-only sandbox
findings.whyItBreaks: Without `-s read-only`, `codex exec` loads the user's Codex configuration and may run with `workspace-write` or `danger-full-access`. Repository-controlled content can therefore induce the review agent to modify the working tree or execute commands with write access, violating the reviewer's read-only security boundary.

findings.title: Restore the explicit read-only sandbox
findings.whyItBreaks: The spawned Codex process now inherits its sandbox mode from CLI defaults or user configuration. Because it runs with the reviewed repository as its working directory, a workspace-write or danger-full-access configuration permits an untrusted review prompt or repository instruction to modify source files or execute repository-controlled code. Prompt instructions prohibiting writes are not a security boundary.

findings.title: Diff the declared PR head from its merge base
findings.whyItBreaks: The bundle and GitHub review target `headSha`, but the patch and changed-file set now target checkout `HEAD` directly from `baseSha`. If the base branch advanced after the PR diverged and HEAD is the PR head, `git diff baseSha HEAD` includes reversed base-only changes as review material. If Actions checked out a merge commit, HEAD differs from `PR_HEAD_SHA`, so reviewed content and inline-comment line positions can differ from the commit passed to GitHub. This can produce false findings or make inline comments fail and fall back to a summary-only review.

findings.title: Restore merge-base semantics for the PR diff
findings.whyItBreaks: PR_BASE_SHA can be the current target-branch tip rather than the PR branch point. If the target branch advanced after the PR branched, `git diff baseSha HEAD` includes inverse changes for target-only commits, so the reviewer reports on files the PR did not change. Passing the same base tip to changedFileSet also makes unrelated files eligible for inline findings.

findings.title: Diff against the resolved PR head SHA
findings.whyItBreaks: The adapter resolves `headSha` from PR_HEAD_SHA but now ignores it when generating the patch. When Actions has a synthetic merge commit, stale checkout, or another commit at HEAD, Needlefish reviews that checkout while posting the review and check run against `headSha`, producing findings for the wrong content and potentially invalid inline locations.

findings.title: Restore the PR merge-base-to-head diff
findings.whyItBreaks: The patch now compares the base-tip SHA with the checkout's HEAD instead of comparing the merge base with the configured PR head SHA. If the base branch advanced after the PR branched and HEAD is the PR head, base-only commits appear as reversed PR changes. If Actions checked out a merge or other commit, the reviewed patch can differ from headSha even though the resulting review is posted against headSha. Needlefish can therefore review unrelated changes, miss actual PR changes, or generate inline comments for the wrong commit.

findings.title: Restore callbacks for literal prompt substitution
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace interprets `$&`, `$` followed by a backtick, `$'`, and `$$` inside a string replacement. Because bundle.patch and generated findings contain arbitrary source text, these sequences are substituted, duplicated, or collapsed before runCodex receives them. The reviewer and critic can therefore analyze text different from the actual diff and return an incorrect verdict.

findings.title: Preserve dynamic prompt payloads as literal text
findings.whyItBreaks: String replacement values interpret sequences such as `$&`, `$`` and `$'`. A legitimate patch containing `$&`, for example, is therefore changed into `{{BUNDLE}}` in the review prompt and `{{PATCH}}` in the critic prompt instead of being passed verbatim. The same corruption applies to serialized candidate findings. Both Codex passes can consequently review text different from the submitted diff and return an incorrect verdict.

findings.title: Preserve prompt substitutions as literal text
findings.whyItBreaks: String.replace interprets `$&`, "$`", "$'", and `$$` in string replacements. Because bundle.patch and candidate findings contain arbitrary source text, those sequences are replaced with the placeholder, surrounding prompt text, or a modified dollar sign. The candidate and critic therefore receive corrupted JSON or patches and can produce an incorrect review.

findings.title: Preserve the analyzed SHA in the fallback review
findings.whyItBreaks: GitHub defaults an omitted commit_id to the pull request's most recent commit. If the PR advances after headSha is captured and reviewed, the fallback now attaches that stale COMMENT or REQUEST_CHANGES verdict to the new head, even though the patch analyzed at lines 143-145 did not include it. This path is particularly reachable when stale inline-comment positions make the first request fail.

findings.title: Keep fallback reviews pinned to the analyzed SHA
findings.whyItBreaks: When the initial review request fails, the fallback now omits commit_id. GitHub defaults an omitted commit_id to the pull request's most recent commit. If the PR advances while Needlefish analyzes headSha, the fallback attaches its stale verdict to the new, unanalyzed commit; a stale REQUEST_CHANGES review can therefore block the updated PR as though it reviewed that revision.

findings.title: Keep the fallback review pinned to the reviewed head
findings.whyItBreaks: When the primary review request fails and the PR head has advanced since headSha was captured, omitting commit_id makes GitHub default the fallback review to the PR's latest commit. The body and verdict were computed from headSha, so a REQUEST_CHANGES verdict can be attached to a newer commit that Needlefish never reviewed. The check run remains pinned to the old head at line 184, producing inconsistent review and check results.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of fabricating them
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview accepts untyped external data and passes each entry here. An object such as {} now becomes a seemingly real P1 bug with an empty file, line 0, and empty explanation instead of raising a validation error. Invalid line strings can also produce NaN. Consumers cannot distinguish these fabricated values from genuine findings, so malformed model output can be reported as a real merge-blocking defect.

findings.title: Preserve the public strict normalization option
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview previously exposed a second strict parameter. TypeScript callers passing false now fail compilation because the exported signature accepts only one argument. JavaScript callers still passing false have the argument silently ignored and receive fabricated fallback findings where the documented implementation previously dropped malformed entries.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of fabricating defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid severity/category values and missing file, line, title, explanation, or fix fields previously produced an error. They now become an indistinguishable Finding with values such as P1, bug, an empty file, and line 0. normalizeReview consequently returns malformed input as a real finding, so callers cannot detect parser failure or safely treat the result as validated.

findings.title: Preserve the public lenient-mode parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview is exported and previously accepted strict=false to discard malformed findings. Removing that parameter makes existing TypeScript calls fail with an extra-argument error; JavaScript callers can still pass false, but it is ignored and malformed entries are retained or null entries throw.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of manufacturing defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid severity/category and missing required fields previously produced an error. They now become a P1 bug with an empty file, line 0, and empty explanation/fix. Because normalizeFinding is exported and returns Finding, callers cannot distinguish normalization failure from a legitimate finding and may display or persist fabricated review results.

findings.title: Preserve the normalizeReview strict parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported function previously accepted normalizeReview(raw, false), which filtered malformed findings. Removing the second parameter breaks existing TypeScript callers at compile time; JavaScript callers still passing false silently receive fabricated default findings instead of having malformed entries omitted.

findings.title: Restore the repository argument for manual dispatch
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty, so these commands run before actions/checkout. At that point gh has neither a checked-out repository nor GH_REPO from which to infer the target repository. Both `gh pr view` calls therefore fail or may resolve against stale self-hosted-runner state, preventing the requested PR refs from being resolved reliably.

findings.title: Restore explicit repository selection for manual runs
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty, so these commands run before actions/checkout. Without -R or GH_REPO, gh must infer the repository from a local Git checkout, which a fresh self-hosted workspace does not have and a reused workspace may resolve from stale state. Repository-resolution failures occur inside echo command substitutions, so echo can still write empty head/base outputs and succeed; checkout then does not select the requested PR SHA.

findings.title: Restore explicit repository selection for manual dispatches
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty, so these commands run before any checkout. Without -R or GH_REPO, gh requires a local repository to determine which repository owns PR_NUM. A clean self-hosted workspace therefore cannot resolve the PR. Additionally, placing the failing command substitution inside echo masks gh's nonzero status and can write empty head/base outputs, so checkout cannot reliably select the PR head.

findings.title: Preserve malformed-review errors
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported function previously rejected non-objects and missing or incorrectly typed summary, findings, checked, and residual_risks fields. It now maps those failures to empty strings or arrays, forcing callers to treat malformed review output as a legitimate review with no findings or risks.

findings.title: Preserve rejection of malformed review output
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported function previously propagated an error when the review or any required top-level field was malformed. It now converts those failures to an empty summary and empty arrays, making malformed output indistinguishable from a legitimate review with no findings or residual risks. Every public caller is therefore forced to treat parsing/validation failure as real review data.

findings.title: Preserve malformed-review failures
findings.whyItBreaks: This exported function previously rejected non-object reviews and missing or incorrectly typed summary, findings, checked, and residual_risks fields. It now converts every such failure into empty strings or arrays, making malformed producer output indistinguishable from a valid review with no findings or residual risks. Every caller is therefore forced to treat failed review generation as a legitimate empty result.

findings.title: Resolve the requested PR head before checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: For workflow_dispatch, github.event.pull_request.head.sha is absent, so this expression selects github.ref—the branch or tag used to dispatch the workflow—not the head of the PR identified by pr_number. The final step executes src/cli.ts from that checkout, causing a manually requested review to use unrelated source; lines 45-46 likewise receive empty event-only SHAs.

findings.title: Restore PR ref resolution for manual dispatches
findings.whyItBreaks: A workflow_dispatch event has no pull_request payload, so the expression selects github.ref—the branch used to dispatch the workflow—not the head of inputs.pr_number. Lines 35, 45, and 46 likewise default the base to main and pass empty PR SHAs. Consequently a manual request installs and runs Needlefish from the wrong revision and cannot reliably compare the requested PR's actual base and head.

findings.title: Restore PR ref resolution for manual reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: A workflow_dispatch event has no pull_request object. The checkout therefore falls back to github.ref, BASE_REF falls back to main, and PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA become empty. The required pr_number is only passed to the CLI and no longer determines the checked-out tool or comparison refs, so a manual run can review an unrelated commit and cannot receive the selected PR's base/head SHAs.

findings.title: Restore the enlarged buffer for Git output
findings.whyItBreaks: runLocal captures the complete `git diff` at line 100. With `maxBuffer` omitted, spawnSync uses Node's 1 MiB default; a larger patch terminates the child with ENOBUFS, leaves status nonzero/null, and triggers the throw at line 12 before any review occurs. The previous 64 MiB limit supported these legitimate diffs.

findings.title: Restore the larger buffer for git diff output
findings.whyItBreaks: runLocal captures the entire patch through git(["diff", ...]) at line 100. Without maxBuffer, spawnSync uses Node's 1 MiB default; larger diffs terminate with ENOBUFS and status=null, so line 12 throws before review(bundle) runs. The previous 64 MiB limit supported these reviews.

findings.title: Restore the larger buffer for full repository diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: runLocal passes the complete `git diff` output through this helper at line 100. With `maxBuffer` omitted, spawnSync uses Node's 1 MiB default; larger patches terminate with ENOBUFS and a null status, so the status guard throws and the review never runs. The previous 64 MiB limit explicitly supported these patches.

findings.title: Keep review exceptions merge-blocking
findings.whyItBreaks: GitHub treats `neutral` as successful for required status checks. If `review(bundle)` throws, the completed Needlefish check therefore satisfies branch protection even though no review result exists and the check output explicitly says the PR did not pass.

findings.title: Keep review errors merge-blocking
findings.whyItBreaks: A GitHub check conclusion of `neutral` satisfies required-check gating. If review generation or review posting throws, the Needlefish check therefore permits merging even though its own summary says the PR did not pass. The previous `failure` conclusion correctly kept that error path merge-blocking.

findings.title: Keep review errors as failed check runs
findings.whyItBreaks: GitHub treats a neutral required status check as satisfying branch protection. If review throws, this now publishes Needlefish as neutral, so a PR can remain mergeable despite the accompanying message saying the review did not pass. The unchanged nonzero process exit does not repair the separately published check-run conclusion.

findings.title: Select the repository explicitly when fetching the PR diff
findings.whyItBreaks: Unlike the surrounding API calls, `gh pr diff` receives neither `--repo` nor `cwd`. It resolves the numbered PR from the process working directory, not from the `cwd` argument or `GITHUB_REPOSITORY`. Calling the exported adapter with a repository path different from the process directory therefore fails or reviews the same-numbered PR from the wrong repository.

findings.title: Restore the trusted tool checkout before executing the reviewer
findings.whyItBreaks: The checkout at lines 43-47 places the untrusted PR head in GITHUB_WORKSPACE. The install step can execute PR-controlled dependency lifecycle scripts, and line 59 directly executes PR-controlled src/cli.ts while GH_TOKEN has pull-requests:write and checks:write permissions. A same-repository PR can therefore run arbitrary code on the persistent self-hosted runner, steal the token, and forge review/check results.

findings.title: Do not run the reviewer from files absent from this repository
findings.whyItBreaks: The head tree contains neither package.json nor src/cli.ts; it only contains .github/workflows/review.yml and .needlefish/answers.json. Consequently the root install cannot provision ./node_modules/.bin/tsx, and the review command cannot find src/cli.ts, so every review job fails instead of posting a review.

facts.meaning: The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.

findings.title: Restore the trusted tool checkout before executing reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: The checkout now places the PR head at the workspace root, after which both pnpm lifecycle hooks and src/cli.ts come from that untrusted revision. The CLI receives GITHUB_TOKEN with pull-requests:write and checks:write permissions, so a PR can replace it to forge its own review/check result or misuse the token. It also gains arbitrary code execution on the persistent self-hosted runner. workflow_dispatch can select a fork PR because its job condition bypasses the same-repository check.

findings.title: Run the reviewer from a trusted checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The checkout is now the PR head, and `pnpm install` executes its package lifecycle scripts on a self-hosted runner. The subsequent command also executes the PR's `src/cli.ts` with a GITHUB_TOKEN that has pull-request and checks write access. A PR can therefore forge its own review result or compromise the persistent runner; workflow_dispatch can additionally select a fork PR because that event bypasses the same-repository condition.

findings.title: Restore the checkout that contains the reviewer
findings.whyItBreaks: The checked-out head contains neither `package.json`, `node_modules/.bin/tsx`, nor `src/cli.ts`; the repository tree at the supplied head only contains `.github/workflows/review.yml` and `.needlefish/answers.json`. The review step therefore fails with a missing executable instead of producing a review. The previous workflow obtained these files from the separate `frankekn/needlefish` checkout.

findings.title: Preserve severity normalization and the fail-safe default
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview passes raw external finding objects into this exported normalizer. Values previously normalized successfully, such as "p0" or " P0 ", now fail the exact membership check and become P3. Missing or malformed severity also changed from the conservative P1 fallback to P3. Consequently, serious findings can be returned as the lowest severity.

findings.title: Preserve severity normalization before validation
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview accepts untyped external data and passes each finding here. Values such as "p0" or " P1 ", which the previous implementation normalized to valid severities, now fail the exact membership check and become P3. This can materially understate a critical finding in the normalized review.

findings.title: Restore canonicalization and the conservative severity fallback
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview accepts untyped runtime data and passes every finding here. Inputs such as "p1" or " P2 ", which were previously canonicalized, now fail the exact membership check and become P3. Missing or invalid severities also changed from P1 to P3. Because the fallback is indistinguishable from a genuine P3, malformed high-severity findings are silently downgraded.

findings.title: Restore GitHub credential scrubbing
findings.whyItBreaks: Without an explicit sanitized env, spawnSync inherits process.env. The Codex subprocess reviewing attacker-controlled repository content can therefore read GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, or GITHUB_API_TOKEN; the read-only filesystem sandbox does not protect environment variables or prevent credential-backed GitHub access.

findings.title: Restore GitHub credential stripping
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the sanitized env argument makes spawnSync inherit process.env, including GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN. The Codex subprocess examines potentially hostile repository content and can execute commands, so prompt injection or a compromised CODEX_BIN can read and exfiltrate credentials or use them for unauthorized GitHub operations. The read-only filesystem sandbox does not protect inherited environment secrets.

findings.title: Restore GitHub credential scrubbing for the child process
findings.whyItBreaks: Omitting the explicit environment makes spawnSync inherit process.env. Consequently GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN are available to the Codex child and any command it runs while inspecting opts.repoPath. Repository-controlled instructions can therefore read and disclose credentials; the read-only filesystem sandbox does not remove environment variables.

findings.title: Restore the fork guard before executing PR code
findings.whyItBreaks: Fork pull requests now reach this self-hosted job. The workflow checks out the contributor-controlled head, runs its pnpm lifecycle scripts, and executes its src/cli.ts, giving arbitrary PR code access to the persistent runner host. The removed predicate previously rejected fork heads because their repository name differs from github.repository.

findings.title: Restore the fork guard before running PR code
findings.whyItBreaks: After this deletion, any fork pull request can start the job on the self-hosted runner. The job checks out the attacker's head SHA, runs dependency installation scripts, and executes src/cli.ts from that checkout. A malicious contributor therefore gains arbitrary code execution on the persistent runner, enabling host compromise and theft of credentials or data retained by other jobs.

findings.title: Restore the same-repository guard
findings.whyItBreaks: A fork PR can now schedule this self-hosted job. The job checks out the fork's head SHA, runs its dependency installation at line 28, and executes its src/cli.ts at line 34. An attacker can therefore run arbitrary code on the persistent runner, access runner-resident credentials or state, and compromise later jobs.

findings.title: Preserve zero as a valid runner delay
findings.whyItBreaks: For either runner delay environment variable, the previously valid value "0" now fails the parser predicate and becomes the fallback. NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 therefore waits 5000 ms before SIGKILL instead of escalating immediately, while NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 waits 2000 ms before resolving instead of finishing immediately.

findings.title: Preserve zero-duration runner overrides
findings.whyItBreaks: A configured value of "0" previously produced a valid zero-delay timer. It now returns the fallback, so NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 waits 5000 ms before SIGKILL and NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 waits 2000 ms before resolving. Existing configurations requesting immediate escalation or completion are silently ignored.

findings.title: Preserve zero-duration timeout settings
findings.whyItBreaks: A configured value of "0" was previously accepted as an immediate timeout stage. It now fails `parsed > 0` and silently becomes the fallback, so `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0` waits 5000 ms before SIGKILL and `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0` waits 2000 ms before resolving. This is an externally visible upgrade regression for existing configurations.

findings.title: Restore deep-review coverage for unmapped files
findings.whyItBreaks: Only the first six mapped hotspots are retained. With the removed uncovered-file backstop, changed files assigned only to later hotspots—or omitted by the mapper—receive no deep review, yet the result can still be returned as complete.

findings.title: Preserve partial results when a deep pass fails
findings.whyItBreaks: A malformed response or execution failure from any single deep pass now rejects reviewLarge immediately. Previously, successful hotspot results were retained and the failed hotspot became a blocking residual risk; large reviews can now fail without producing any review result.

findings.title: Propagate residual risks from deep reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: Every deep pass's residual_risks is discarded and the critic is explicitly given an empty list. A deep reviewer can report unresolved evidence with blocks=true, but that signal can no longer reach the final verdict, allowing an unjustified PASS.

findings.title: Supply exact revisions to the critic prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: The large-review critic receives only a diff stat and no longer substitutes the supplied baseSha and headSha. It therefore lacks the exact revision range needed to inspect or verify changed lines, especially when HEAD's parent is not the PR base.

findings.title: Preserve residual risks from deep passes
findings.whyItBreaks: Every successful deep pass can return blocking residual_risks, but the merge now replaces all of them with an unconditional empty array. The critic therefore cannot distinguish a fully verified review from one with unresolved blocking evidence, and the exported result can omit those risks.

findings.title: Isolate failures from individual hotspot reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex, JSON extraction, or normalization failing for any one hotspot now throws out of reviewLarge. A single malformed deep-pass response prevents every other hotspot result from being returned, whereas the previous behavior continued and reported the failed coverage as a blocking residual risk.

findings.title: Restore deep coverage for unmapped changed files
findings.whyItBreaks: Only the six highest-ranked mapped hotspots are reviewed now. Any changed file omitted by the mapper or present only in a seventh-or-later hotspot receives no deep review and produces no warning, allowing a large PR to be reported clean despite part of its diff never being inspected.

findings.title: Restore coverage for files outside selected hotspots
findings.whyItBreaks: The top-six slice is now the final hotspot list. In a large PR whose changed files are assigned only to lower-ranked hotspots, those files receive no deep review, yet the pipeline can still return a passing ReviewResult.

findings.title: Preserve blocking residual risks from deep reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: Each deep result's residual_risks is discarded and the critic is explicitly given an empty array. A deep pass that reports an unresolved blocking risk can therefore become a PASS when the critic returns no findings, because deriveVerdict only receives the critic's now-lossy result.

findings.title: Keep large reviews alive when one deep pass fails
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex, JSON extraction, or normalization failing for any single hotspot now rejects reviewLarge entirely. Previously the remaining hotspots were reviewed and the failed coverage was returned as a blocking residual risk; one malformed model response now makes the whole large-PR review unavailable.

findings.title: Retain behavioral evidence in the deduplication key
findings.whyItBreaks: Two findings with the same file, starting line, category, and first 60 title characters now collide even when whyItBreaks describes distinct defects. The map keeps only one, silently removing a real issue before the critic sees it.

findings.title: Restore focus propagation for large reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: When review() selects reviewLarge for a patch over 30,000 characters or 10 files, bundle.focus is now omitted from both the mapping input and every deep-review prompt. The small-review path still serializes the complete bundle, so the same explicit focus request works for small PRs but is silently ignored for large PRs.

findings.title: Preserve focus in the large-review prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: When a bundle crosses the large-review threshold, bundle.focus is no longer included in the mapping input, so hotspot selection ignores the requested review scope. The same change also removes focus substitution from the per-hotspot prompt at lines 117-121. Small reviews still serialize the complete bundle, making focus behavior depend incorrectly on patch size.

findings.title: Preserve focus and deep options in large reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: When isLarge(bundle) is true, focus and deep are no longer serialized into the mapping prompt, and focus is no longer substituted into each deep-review prompt at lines 117-121. Consequently, large reviews silently disregard both caller-supplied controls, while reviewSmall still receives the complete bundle; the same public input therefore behaves differently solely because the patch crosses the size threshold.

findings.title: Normalize rounded seconds into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: The code floors minutes before rounding the remainder, so rounding can produce 60 seconds without carrying into minutes. For example, 59,999 ms renders as `60s`, and 119,999 ms renders as `1m 60s`, instead of `1m 0s` and `2m 0s`. These incorrect values appear in both per-call and total-duration review output.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: Minutes are computed before the remaining milliseconds are rounded. A duration of 119500ms therefore renders as `1m 60s` instead of `2m 0s`; this affects both per-call and total durations shown in review output.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into the next minute
findings.whyItBreaks: Rounding occurs after minutes are extracted. For 59,500 ms this returns `60s`, and for 119,500 ms it returns `1m 60s`, instead of carrying the rounded second into the minute count. Both per-call and total durations therefore display incorrectly near every minute boundary.

findings.title: Reject zero in parsePositiveInteger
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported function and its error text promise a positive integer, but the changed predicate accepts "0" and returns 0. Callers relying on successful parsing to establish a value greater than zero therefore receive a value outside the documented contract.

findings.title: Continue rejecting zero as non-positive
findings.whyItBreaks: For input "0", Number(value) produces 0, Number.isInteger(0) is true, and `0 < 0` is false, so the function returns zero. This contradicts both the exported name `parsePositiveInteger` and its positive-integer error contract, forcing public callers to accept a value the API promises to reject.

findings.title: Reject zero as a non-positive integer
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported parser now returns 0, while both its name and error contract promise a positive integer. Public callers relying on a result greater than zero can receive a value outside the documented domain.
